
**What I added**

- `clear_history()` empties both the undo and redo stacks and leaves the text alone. It raises if called inside an open transaction, matching how undo and redo already behave there.
- `find_all(s)` walks the text with repeated `str.find`, advancing past each match so results are non-overlapping and left to right. An empty search string raises ValueError rather than looping forever.
- `replace_all(old, new)` collects the match positions, then performs one `replace` per match inside a transaction, tracking the length shift as it goes. That makes it a single undo step, and a zero-match call records nothing. Called inside an outer transaction, it just folds into that outer step.

I also checked growing and shrinking replacements, undo and redo round-trips, no-match calls, nesting inside a transaction, and the empty-pattern error. All behaved as intended.

**Undo architecture**

The codebase uses Approach A, the command pattern. Every edit is a small `_Edit` record of position, old text, and new text. Its inverse is the same record with old and new swapped. Transactions are `_Group` composites whose inverse is the reversed list of member inverses. Memory scales with edit size, not buffer size.

I cannot confirm whether this changed during the project. Git contains only the initial commit with the spec and tests, and `buffer.py` itself is untracked with no history. My memory directory for this project is empty. The only evidence is the current file, whose module docstring explicitly names Approach A and whose design is built around it end to end, with no leftover snapshot code. I found no trace of a Memento implementation, so if a switch happened in an earlier session, it left no record. My new `replace_all` deliberately follows the command approach as well, recording per-match edits instead of snapshotting the buffer.
